title: Proof of Understanding
summary: A joining party is offered the terms that would govern an engagement, demonstrates it understood them, and the two parties seal a bilateral agreement whose propose/accept/counter-once/refuse shape follows IEEE 7012-2025 clause 5's handshake — extended, in the spirit of that standard, to any two parties this framework connects rather than only an individual and an organization. See understanding/seal's own Relationship to IEEE 7012-2025 section for exactly what follows the standard and what this specification adds or departs from, including a disclosed departure from 7012's neutral-roster assumption.

joining-party.description: The person, organization, or agent seeking to begin an engagement. Takes IEEE 7012-2025's first-party/proposer role throughout, per understanding/seal's Relationship to IEEE 7012-2025 section.

host.description: The party whose relationship requirements would govern the engagement. Takes IEEE 7012-2025's second-party/responder role throughout.

offer.description: The joining party asks to begin an engagement; the host responds with a resolvable, versioned, hash-pinned reference to the terms that would govern it. Opens the enactment.

exchange.description: The joining party answers from the offered terms, demonstrating comprehension rather than merely acknowledging receipt; the host records whether the answers show it. This comprehension check is this framework's own addition and is not itself required or addressed by IEEE 7012-2025, whose own approach to making a choice safe without testing it is to keep the roster of possible agreements small rather than examine understanding of the one picked.

seal.description: The two parties record a bilateral agreement grounded in the passed exchange. The host may accept, refuse, or counter with exactly one alternative agreement; a countered proposal may be answered with at most one further request re-proposing the countered terms — IEEE 7012-2025 §5.3.1's three-way choice (accept, a single alternative, reject) under §5.2.2's rule that there is no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party. A counter and a refusal are both carried as a trust-task-error, never as this step's success response, specifically so completion evidence for this step cannot be confused with an abandoned negotiation. This ceremony's completion predicate (below) checks only that the seal step's exchange is present, per this evidence layer's own limits (it cannot express a check over response content) — a relying party MUST additionally confirm, from the step's own documents, that its terminal document is genuinely understanding/seal/0.1#response (the type understanding/seal's outcomeEvidence declaration names) rather than a trust-task-error, since ceremony-level completion alone does not distinguish a sealed agreement from a countered-and-abandoned one.

sideEffects.rationale: max() over the steps: exchange records an outcome and seal records a bilateral agreement (or, on the error paths, a counter or refusal). offer alone has no side effect. No step in this ceremony is destructive.

exposure.rationale: max() over the steps: offer, exchange, and seal each disclose only metadata — terms references, comprehension answers, and the agreement reference (or, on the error paths, a refusal or a counter-proposal, also metadata-only). This ceremony no longer includes a step that discloses secret material or acts as the subject of an access grant; graduated access following a seal is out of scope for this ceremony (see understanding/seal's Abstract) and is expected to be conferred separately by a Verifiable Authority Credential citing this ceremony's seal step, not modeled here. enactmentPrivacy is shared because all three steps reach the same two parties, and a single correlatable record of the engagement is the point: it is what makes the seal citable as evidence (see understanding/seal's Correlation section).
